3108: The Holy Maccabees were venerated with a feast day (1 August) from early times.
3109: The author describes his work as a condensation of Jason's history and apologises for any shortcomings (2:23-32; 15:37-39).

3112: Preached a panegyric on the Maccabean martyrs as models of endurance.
3114: At Leipzig, Eck used 2 Macc 12 for purgatory; Luther answered that Maccabees is not in the canon.

3132: Greek, in an ornate, florid style.
3133: An Alexandrian Jewish author, telling a story set in Egypt under Ptolemy IV Philopator (221-204 BC).
3134:
Third Maccabees has nothing to do with the Maccabees; the name probably came because it also tells of a pagan king persecuting faithful Jews. After defeating Antiochus III at Raphia (217 BC), Ptolemy IV visits Jerusalem and tries to enter the Holy of Holies, but is struck down after the high priest Simon prays. Back in Egypt he takes revenge: he demands that Jews register and be branded with the ivy leaf of Dionysus, offers citizenship to apostates, and rounds up the Jews of Egypt into the hippodrome to be trampled by drugged elephants.

Three times the plan fails (the king oversleeps, then forgets), and at the last moment, after the priest Eleazar's prayer, two angels appear, the elephants turn on the soldiers, and the king repents and honours the Jews, who institute an annual festival. Josephus tells a similar elephant story but under a later king, Ptolemy VIII, which suggests a shared legend. The book's concern is the fidelity and civic standing of Alexandrian Jews.
3135: A story set in Egypt about 217 BC, in which a Greek king tries to enter the Temple and then to have Egypt's Jews trampled by elephants, until God intervenes. It is called Maccabees only because of its similar theme. It is Scripture for the Orthodox, but not for Catholics, Protestants or Jews.
3136: Battle of Raphia and Ptolemy's attempt to enter the sanctuary (ch. 1-2)
3137: Simon the high priest's prayer and the king struck down (ch. 2)
3138: Persecution of Egyptian Jews: registration, branding, the hippodrome (ch. 2-4)
3139: The elephants and the king's delays (ch. 5)
3140: Eleazar's prayer, two angels and the Jews' deliverance; a new festival (ch. 6-7)
3141:
Jews never received it; it is a Greek work from Egypt and was not transmitted in rabbinic tradition.

Catholics: it was never in the Latin Vulgate and is not in the lists of Hippo, Carthage or Trent, so the Western church never read it as Scripture.

Protestants: outside both the Hebrew canon and the Latin Apocrypha, so it was not even included in the Apocrypha section of Reformation Bibles. Its legendary character (elephants, the king's repeated forgetting) and duplication of a story Josephus places later also count against it historically.
3142:
In the Greek East, 3 Maccabees stood in many Septuagint manuscripts (Codex Alexandrinus contains it) and the Apostolic Canons (canon 85) list three books of Maccabees among the books to be revered. The Greek Orthodox churches therefore count it among the anagignoskomena (books worthy to be read); the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) did not list it separately but its Bibles include it. Some Syriac Peshitta manuscripts also contain it.

Orthodox readers value it as a story of God defending his people in the Diaspora through prayer, closely parallel in spirit to Esther and Daniel.
3143: Old Testament-era story; apostolicity does not apply.
3144: Written in the 1st century BC or AD about events of 217 BC.
3145: Conventional Jewish piety; no doctrinal controversy.
3146: Known almost only in the Greek East and parts of the Syriac church.
3147: Read in Greek Orthodox tradition; little use in the West.
3150: List three books of Maccabees among the books to be held in reverence.
3151: Tells a similar story of Jews exposed to elephants in Alexandria, but under Ptolemy VIII Physcon.
3152: Daniel's vision of the king of the south defeating the king of the north is commonly linked to the Battle of Raphia (217 BC) that opens 3 Maccabees.
3153: Like Esther, the story ends with a planned massacre reversed and an annual festival established.
3154: God sending his angel to shut the lions' mouths parallels the angels who turn the elephants.
3163: Late estimate (after the Bar Kokhba era)
3164: Greek, a philosophical discourse in the style of Stoic diatribe.
3165: A Hellenistic Jew, probably in Antioch or Alexandria; Eusebius and Jerome attributed it to Josephus, which modern scholars reject.
3166:
Fourth Maccabees is a philosophical speech arguing that devout reason is master of the passions. The author first makes the case in general terms, drawing on Greek philosophy but insisting that true reason is trained by the Jewish Law. He then proves it with the examples of the martyrs from 2 Maccabees: the aged priest Eleazar, the seven brothers and their mother, who endure torture rather than eat pork.

The book expands the torture scenes in vivid detail and turns the mother into a hero greater than any philosopher. It also develops the idea that the martyrs' deaths were a ransom and an atoning sacrifice (hilasterion) for the nation's sin (6:28-29; 17:21-22), language strikingly close to how the New Testament speaks of Christ's death. It was very popular among early Christians, who honoured the Maccabean martyrs.
3167: A Jewish philosophical sermon showing that faithful reason can conquer pain and fear, using the Maccabean martyrs as proof. It speaks of their deaths as atoning for the nation. It is printed as an appendix in Greek Bibles but is not Scripture for most churches.
3168: Thesis: devout reason rules the emotions (ch. 1-3)
3170: Eleazar's debate with Antiochus and martyrdom (ch. 5-7)
3171: The seven brothers' torture and steadfastness (ch. 8-14)
3173: Their deaths as ransom; final exhortation (ch. 17-18)
3175: Jews did not transmit it. Catholics never had it in the Vulgate. Protestants did not include it even among the Apocrypha. Its late date, philosophical genre (a sermon rather than history or prophecy) and the mistaken attribution to Josephus all kept it on the margins. Even in the Orthodox churches it is placed as an appendix rather than as a full member of the anagignoskomena.
3176:
It stands in major Greek codices (Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus) and in some Syriac manuscripts (the great Milan Peshitta codex includes it). Greek Orthodox Bibles print it as an appendix. Fathers such as Gregory of Nazianzus and John Chrysostom drew on its portrait of the martyrs, and the feast of the Holy Maccabees is kept on 1 August in both East and West.

Scholars value it highly as a witness to Jewish ideas of vicarious, atoning suffering in the decades when the New Testament was written, and to the meeting of Greek philosophy and Torah.
3177: Jewish work of the New Testament era; not apostolic.
3178: Probably 1st century AD, contemporary with the apostles.
3179: Its Jewish piety is orthodox; its Stoic framing is distinctive.
3180: Known mainly in the Greek and Syriac churches.
3181: Used in sermons on the martyrs; not read as a lectionary book.
3182: Presents itself as a philosophical discourse, not revelation.
3183: Attributes a work On the Sovereignty of Reason (some call it Maccabees) to Josephus.
3185: Preached homilies on the Maccabean martyrs and their mother.
3186: His oration on the Maccabees draws on themes found in 4 Maccabees.
3187: Paul calls Christ a hilasterion (propitiation or mercy seat), the same word 4 Macc 17:22 uses of the martyrs' deaths.
3188: The tortured who refused release are commonly linked to the Maccabean martyrs that 4 Maccabees celebrates.
3189: Endurance before witnesses and looking to the end resemble 4 Maccabees' athletic imagery for the martyrs (4 Macc 17:11-16).
3190: The suffering servant bearing others' sins is the scriptural root of the atoning-death idea both 4 Maccabees and the New Testament develop.
3201: Greek, translated from a Hebrew-Aramaic text of Chronicles-Ezra-Nehemiah that differs from the Masoretic text in places; the contest story may have been composed in Aramaic or Greek.
3202: Jewish translator-editor, probably in Egypt in the 2nd century BC.
3203:
First Esdras retells the history from Josiah's great Passover (2 Chr 35) through the fall of Jerusalem, the return under Cyrus, the rebuilding of the Temple, and Ezra's reading of the Law (Neh 8). Most of it closely parallels canonical Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah, though in a different order and omitting most of Nehemiah's own story.

Its one large new section is the contest of the three bodyguards of King Darius (3:1-5:6): each argues what is strongest, wine, the king, or women; the third, identified as Zerubbabel, adds that truth is greatest of all and wins permission to rebuild Jerusalem. The saying that truth is great and prevails became proverbial in Latin (magna est veritas). Josephus followed 1 Esdras rather than canonical Ezra for this period. In Latin Bibles it is called 3 Esdras (Ezra and Nehemiah being 1 and 2 Esdras), which causes endless confusion of names.
3204: A Greek retelling of the end of Chronicles plus Ezra and parts of Nehemiah, with an added story of three guards debating what is strongest, won by the answer: truth. The Orthodox count it as Scripture; Catholics print it only in an appendix; Protestants list it among the Apocrypha.
3205: Josiah's Passover and the last kings of Judah (ch. 1)
3206: Cyrus' decree and the first return; opposition to rebuilding (ch. 2)
3207: Contest of the three guards: wine, king, women, truth (3:1-5:6)
3208: Return under Zerubbabel and the rebuilding of the Temple (5:7-7:15)
3209: Ezra's mission and the mixed marriages crisis (ch. 8-9)
3210: Ezra reads the Law to the people (9:37-55)
3211:
Jews: it duplicates material from the Hebrew Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah; Jews kept the Hebrew forms.

Catholics: Trent omitted it from the canon (it was not clearly distinguished in earlier lists and Jerome had not translated it). The Clementine Vulgate (1592) printed it in an appendix after the New Testament, with the Prayer of Manasseh and 4 Esdras, so that it would not be lost.

Protestants: Article VI lists it (as the Third Book of Esdras) among books read for example only; Luther left it out of his Apocrypha; Reformed churches reject it. The main objections are that it duplicates canonical books in a confused order (for example it puts the Artaxerxes correspondence before Darius) and that the contest story is a legend.
3212:
It was in the Greek Bible (as Esdras A, before the canonical Ezra-Nehemiah, which was Esdras B). Many scholars think the two Esdras books listed at Hippo and Carthage include it. The Orthodox read it among the anagignoskomena, and the Ethiopian church includes an Ezra book generally identified with it in its broader canon (identification debated).

It is valued as an independent witness to the text and history of the return from exile, and for its celebration of truth as belonging to God. Augustine read the contest's praise of truth as pointing to Christ, who is the Truth.
3213: A 2nd-century BC translation of older material; the contest story is later.
3214: Its theology matches the canonical books it parallels.
3215: Read in the Greek East; marginal in the Latin West after Jerome.
3216: Used by Fathers and by Josephus; read in Orthodox tradition.
3217: Makes no prophetic claim of its own.
3218: Follows 1 Esdras, including the contest of the guards, in his account of the return.
3219: Discusses Ezra's contest of the youths and reads the victory of truth as a prophecy of Christ.
3221: Printed 3 Esdras in an appendix after Trent excluded it, so that it should not perish entirely.
3222: Josiah's Passover, with which 1 Esdras opens.
3224: The opposition to rebuilding, which 1 Esdras places in a different order.
3225: Ezra's public reading of the Law, which forms the ending of 1 Esdras.
3226: Jesus calls himself the truth; Christian readers linked this to the contest's praise of truth.
3240: Core (4 Ezra) probably Hebrew, then Greek, both lost; survives in Latin, Syriac, Ethiopic, Georgian, Arabic, Armenian and Coptic fragments. Chapters 1-2 and 15-16 are Christian additions in Latin.
3241: The core is a Jewish apocalypse written about AD 100 in the land of Israel, in response to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70; the outer chapters were added by Christians in the 2nd-3rd centuries.
3242:
Second Esdras in English Bibles is a composite. Its heart, chapters 3-14 (called 4 Ezra by scholars), is one of the most searching Jewish writings ever produced. Set thirty years after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem (a stand-in for Rome in AD 70), Ezra wrestles with the angel Uriel in seven visions: why does God let Israel suffer under worse sinners? Why did God not remove the evil heart from Adam? Why will so few be saved? Uriel answers that human minds cannot grasp God's ways, that the age is hastening to its end, and that the world to come is made for the few. Later visions show a mourning woman transformed into a city (Zion), an eagle (Rome) rebuked by a lion (the Messiah), and a man rising from the sea who destroys the nations with the fire of his mouth. Finally Ezra, by inspiration, dictates 94 books: 24 to publish (the Hebrew Bible) and 70 to keep for the wise.

Chapters 1-2 (5 Ezra) are a Christian prophecy of God rejecting Israel for a new people, and 15-16 (6 Ezra) are Christian oracles of woe. Chapter 7 speaks of God's son the Messiah who will reign 400 years and then die, before the resurrection. A long passage (7:36-105) about the intermediate state was missing from most Latin copies until Robert Bensly published it in 1875 from a manuscript found at Amiens.
3243: A Jewish book written about AD 100, after Rome destroyed Jerusalem, in which Ezra argues with an angel about why God lets his people suffer and why so few are saved; Christians later added chapters at the beginning and end. It is in the Ethiopian Bible and in Catholic and Anglican appendices, but is Scripture almost nowhere else.
3244: 5 Ezra: God turns from Israel to a new people (ch. 1-2, Christian)
3245: Visions 1-3: dialogues with Uriel on evil, Adam's sin and the few who are saved (3:1-9:25)
3246: The Messiah's 400-year reign and the intermediate state of souls (ch. 7)
3247: Vision 4: the mourning woman becomes the new Zion (9:26-10:59)
3248: Vision 5: the eagle and the lion (ch. 11-12)
3249: Vision 6: the man from the sea (ch. 13)
3250: Vision 7: Ezra restores the 24 public and 70 hidden books (ch. 14)
3251: 6 Ezra: oracles of judgement on the nations (ch. 15-16, Christian)
3252:
Jews: written after AD 70 and preserved only by Christians; the rabbis did not transmit apocalypses of this kind.

Catholics: Trent excluded it; the Clementine Vulgate printed it as 4 Esdras in the appendix.

Protestants: obviously late and pseudonymous (Ezra lived in the 5th century BC), with Christian interpolations, a Messiah who dies after 400 years, and a claim that Ezra re-wrote the lost Scriptures by inspiration. Article VI lists it as the Fourth Book of Esdras for reading only; Luther excluded it.

Orthodox: absent from the Greek Bible; included as 3 Esdras in the Slavonic (Russian) Bible, so its standing is that of an appendix and is debated.
3253:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts it (as Ezra Sutuel) in its canon. Latin Christians quoted it widely: Ambrose used it, and the Catholic liturgy for the dead borrowed its words: eternal rest grant them and let perpetual light shine on them (the Requiem introit, from 2:34-35), and the Easter-time introit about the joy of glory comes from 2:36-37.

Readers of every tradition value 4 Ezra as an honest theodicy: it lets a faithful man voice grief and protest to God, much as Job and Lamentations do, and it is a key witness to Jewish messianic hope, beliefs about Adam's sin and the afterlife in the generation of the New Testament.
3254: Pseudonymous Ezra; the Christian chapters are not apostolic either.
3255: Composed c. AD 100, well after the prophetic era.
3256: Its theodicy is profound; its dying Messiah and fixed timetables were unusual for later doctrine.
3257: Kept in the Ethiopian canon and Latin appendices only.
3258: Used in Latin liturgy (Requiem) and by Ambrose; read in Ethiopia.
3259: Strongly claims revelation through visions and an inspired Ezra (ch. 14).
3260: Quoted Esdras (4 Ezra) with respect in his writings on death and the soul.
3262: Its entrance chant, eternal rest and perpetual light, is drawn from 2 Esdras 2:34-35.
3264: Published the missing fragment 7:36-105 from a Latin manuscript discovered at Amiens.
3265: Printed 4 Esdras in an appendix after Trent excluded it.
3266: Paul on sin entering through Adam is often compared with 4 Ezra 7:118 (O Adam, what have you done?).
3267: Souls under the altar asking how long resemble the souls in their chambers asking when the harvest comes (4 Ezra 4:35-37).
3268: The man rising from the sea in 4 Ezra 13 reinterprets Daniel's one like a son of man.
3269: The new Jerusalem revealed resembles the mourning woman transformed into a city in 4 Ezra 10.
3270: Jesus' saying that few find the narrow way parallels 4 Ezra's theme that few are saved (4 Ezra 8:1-3).
3271: Ezra the scribe reading the Law, the historical root of 4 Ezra's picture of Ezra as restorer of Scripture.
3282: Greek as we have it (possibly from a Hebrew or Aramaic original). A different Hebrew prayer attributed to Manasseh was found at Qumran (4Q381).
3283: A Jewish author composing the penitential prayer that 2 Chronicles says Manasseh prayed; first attested in the Christian Didascalia Apostolorum (3rd century).
3284:
This fifteen-verse prayer is put in the mouth of King Manasseh of Judah, the most wicked king in Kings, who according to Chronicles was taken to Babylon in chains, humbled himself and prayed, and was restored. The Chronicler mentions that his prayer was recorded in the records of the seers, and this text fills that gap.

It moves from praise of the Creator who bound the sea, to the confession that God has appointed repentance for sinners, to a deeply personal confession (I have sinned more than the number of the sands of the sea; I bend the knee of my heart), and ends with a plea for forgiveness and a promise of lifelong praise. It is one of the finest penitential prayers in Jewish and Christian literature, and is used in Orthodox Great Compline and as an Anglican canticle.
3285: A short, moving prayer of repentance written in the name of King Manasseh, the worst king of Judah, who the Bible says repented in exile. It fills in the prayer that 2 Chronicles mentions but does not quote. Most churches value it for devotion, but few count it as Scripture.
3286: Praise of God the Creator, before whom all tremble (v. 1-5)
3287: God's mercy has appointed repentance for sinners (v. 6-8)
3288: Confession: sins more numerous than the sand (v. 9-10)
3289: I bend the knee of my heart: plea for forgiveness (v. 11-13)
3290: Promise of praise all the days of life (v. 14-15)
3291:
Jews never received it; its first attestation is in a Christian church order.

Catholics: Trent did not include it; the Clementine Vulgate printed it in the appendix.

Protestants: Article VI lists it among the Apocrypha, and Luther printed it as the last book of his Apocrypha; Reformed churches reject it. The reasons are its late attestation, absence from the Hebrew Bible, and the fact that it is a composition supplying a prayer Scripture only mentions. Some Protestants also note that the Chronicles account of Manasseh's repentance is absent from Kings, so the prayer builds on a debated episode.

Orthodox: it is among the Odes appended to the Psalter in Greek Bibles and used liturgically; its formal status is sometimes described as appendix rather than full deuterocanon (debated).
3292: It is valued almost everywhere as a model of repentance and of God's mercy toward the worst of sinners. The Didascalia and the Apostolic Constitutions quote it in full to show bishops how to receive penitents. Codex Alexandrinus includes it among the Odes. The Ethiopian church includes it within its Chronicles. It is prayed in Orthodox Compline and was placed among the canticles of the Church of England.
3293: Old Testament-era prayer; apostolicity does not apply.
3294: Probably 2nd-1st century BC, first attested in the 3rd century AD.
3295: Classic biblical theology of sin, repentance and mercy.
3296: Used devotionally across many churches but formally canonical in few.
3297: Prayed in liturgy (Orthodox Compline, Anglican canticles).
3298: Presented as Manasseh's own prayer; most scholars regard this as a literary attribution.
3300: Quotes the whole prayer in teaching bishops to receive repentant sinners.
3302: Repeats the Didascalia's use of the prayer.
3303: Includes the prayer among the Odes after the Psalms.
3304: Printed it in a separate section between the Testaments of his 1534 German Bible, headed as books not held equal to Holy Scripture but useful and good to read.
3305: Printed it in an appendix after Trent omitted it from the canon list.
3306: Manasseh humbles himself in distress and prays, and God restores him to Jerusalem.
3307: His prayer is said to be written in the records of the kings and of the seers; the Prayer of Manasseh fills this gap.
3308: Kings records Manasseh's great sins without any repentance.
3309: The prodigal son's confession is often compared with the prayer's spirit.
3313: Psalm of David outside the number
3317: Hebrew original, now attested in the Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (11Q5, column 28); also Greek, Syriac, Latin, Ethiopic.
3318: A Jewish poet writing in David's voice; the Greek version is a condensed combination of two Hebrew psalms.
3319:
Psalm 151 is a short autobiographical poem in David's voice, labelled in the Septuagint as written by David himself and outside the number (of the 150 psalms). David says he was small among his brothers and a shepherd; his hands made a harp; God sent his messenger and anointed him rather than his handsome brothers; and he went out against the Philistine, cut off his head with his own sword and removed reproach from Israel.

Until 1956 it was known only in translation. The Psalms Scroll from Qumran then revealed a longer Hebrew original, actually two psalms (151A on David's anointing and 151B on Goliath), which the Greek had compressed. The same scroll contains other non-canonical psalms (numbered 152-155 in Syriac Bibles), showing that the outer edge of the Psalter was still fluid in some Jewish circles around the time of Jesus.
